title: Secure Autonomous Agent Payments: Verifying Authenticity and Intent in a Trustless Environment
summary: Proposes a blockchain-based framework for AI-initiated payments that uses DIDs and verifiable credentials for agent identity, on-chain intent proofs recording user authorization, zero-knowledge proofs for private policy compliance and TEE attestations of agent execution, with a hybrid on-chain and off-chain audit trail; the evaluation is qualitative.
whyItMatters: An early sketch of the intent-binding and identity-attestation ideas that ap2 mandates and erc-8004 validation later formalize.

title: Personhood credentials: Artificial intelligence and the value of privacy-preserving tools to distinguish who is real online
summary: Analyzes personhood credentials, privacy-preserving digital credentials that let users prove to online services that they are real people without revealing personal information, issued by governments or other trusted institutions, and discusses benefits, deployment risks and design challenges as AI becomes indistinguishable from humans online.
whyItMatters: The complement to agent identity: visa-tap and openai-acp need to tell delegated agents from both humans and malicious bots, and personhood credentials sit at one end of that spectrum.

title: Evaluating LLM Agent Collusion in Double Auctions
summary: Places LLM sellers in simulated continuous double auctions and tests when they collude, defined as secret cooperation that harms another party. Direct seller communication increases collusion, propensity differs by model, and oversight or urgency from authority figures changes collusive behavior.
whyItMatters: Relevant to any multi-seller agent market on ACP, UCP or x402: giving seller agents a channel to talk to each other is itself a competition risk.

title: AI agents for cash management in payment systems
summary: Tests whether a general-purpose reasoning model, prompted with simulated scenarios, can manage intraday liquidity in a wholesale payment system; the agent keeps precautionary buffers and prioritizes payments much like a human cash manager without domain training. Published by the BIS on 2025-11-26; a journal version appeared in the Journal of Financial Market Infrastructures in 2026 (DOI 10.21314/jfmi.2026.008).
whyItMatters: Central bank evidence that agents can operate inside payment infrastructure itself, not only at checkout; it frames the supervisory questions that wholesale agent payments would raise.

title: Evolution of Market Microstructure in the Age of AI
summary: A survey tracing market microstructure from floor trading through electronic order books, batch auctions, dark pools and blockchain automated market makers to AI agents that discover, pay for and compete over resources, organized around whether a market can allocate efficiently without participants revealing everything. It argues that allocation is the missing layer of the agent-commerce protocol stack.
whyItMatters: Positions payment protocols such as x402 and MPP as settlement without allocation, and names extractable value and algorithmic collusion as the next problems for agent markets.

title: What Is Your AI Agent Buying? Evaluation, Biases, Model Dependence, & Emerging Implications for Agentic E-Commerce
summary: Using ACES, a provider-agnostic framework for auditing agent decisions, the authors measure how LLM shopping agents choose among products. They find demand concentrating on a few modal products, preferences that reshuffle with model updates, strong position biases that persist even in text-only interfaces, and consistent reactions to sponsored tags and platform endorsements.
whyItMatters: Checkout protocols such as OpenAI ACP and UCP move the purchase decision into an agent; this paper quantifies the ranking and position biases merchants and platforms inherit when the agent, not a person, picks the product. Agentic Commerce Protocol (ACP): How agents choose products, relevant to feed-driven discovery in ChatGPT. UCP: Shows how agent buyers are biased by placement and model choice, which matters for platform checkout.

title: Beyond the Mandate: A Systematic Security Analysis of the Agent Payments Protocol (AP2)
summary: Systematic security analysis of AP2 v0.2 across five lifecycle phases and five deployment architectures, using MAESTRO threat modeling to catalog 48 threats in five families and AIVSS scoring to flag eight High-band threats, each demonstrated on a purpose-built testbed with proofs of concept and mitigations, plus a deployment-aware scanner. The central finding is that valid mandate signatures do not guarantee that a transaction reflects user intent when the pre-authorization context is manipulated.
whyItMatters: Most complete threat catalog for ap2 to date, and it covers the A2A and MCP inputs that sit outside the signed mandates. AP2: The main security analysis of AP2 v0.2; source of the 48-threat count in section H.

title: Magentic Marketplace: An Open-Source Environment for Studying Agentic Markets
summary: Introduces Magentic-Marketplace, an open-source simulated two-sided market in which assistant agents represent consumers and service agents represent competing businesses, and uses it to measure utility, behavioral bias, vulnerability to manipulation and the effect of search mechanisms. Frontier models approach optimal welfare only under ideal search, degrade sharply with scale, and show a severe first-proposal bias that gives response speed a 10 to 30 times advantage over quality.
whyItMatters: Discovery and checkout protocols such as UCP and OpenAI ACP create the two-sided agent markets this environment simulates, so its first-proposal and search findings bear directly on how merchant feeds and ranking should be designed. Agentic Commerce Protocol (ACP): Simulated agent marketplaces; context for agent-mediated checkout. UCP: Simulated agentic marketplaces; useful to reason about many platforms meeting many businesses.

title: Epistemic Sybil Resistance: Multiplying AI Agents Without Multiplying Evidence
summary: Formalizes an epistemic Sybil problem: extra agent reports that descend from the same evidence add no information, and report-only aggregators cannot tell replication from independent corroboration. Experiments show naive posterior coverage collapsing from 0.940 to 0.263 as report count rises on a single evidence root, and the author argues that aggregation should track evidential ancestry rather than agent or report count.
whyItMatters: Reframes Sybil resistance for ERC-8004 style feedback and validation: many attestations from agents sharing a base model or data source should not be counted as independent evidence.

title: Provable Security Analysis of FIDO2
summary: Gives the first provable-security analysis of FIDO2, covering WebAuthn and the CTAP2 authenticator protocol; it proves security properties of WebAuthn, finds weaknesses in CTAP2 and proposes a stronger replacement.
whyItMatters: Passkey and FIDO-based consent is how card networks propose to confirm a cardholder before an agent pays; this paper pins down what the underlying protocol does and does not guarantee.

title: The EMV Standard: Break, Fix, Verify
venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy 2021
summary: Builds a Tamarin model of the EMV contactless protocol and finds that unauthenticated card data lets an attacker bypass the PIN for high-value Visa contactless payments; the authors propose and verify fixes that terminals can deploy.
whyItMatters: The method, formal modeling of a payment network protocol that exposes a deployable attack, is what recent work applies to agent payment specs; it also shows how fragile unauthenticated fields are.

title: Card Brand Mixup Attack: Bypassing the PIN in non-Visa Cards by Using Them for Visa Transactions
summary: Shows that an attacker can make a terminal treat a Mastercard contactless card as a Visa card, routing the transaction so that the earlier Visa PIN bypass applies; the authors demonstrated it with an Android app in real transactions.
whyItMatters: A mismatch between card brand and network routing breaks assumptions on both sides; agent payment designs that span Visa and Mastercard credentials must bind the brand and network explicitly.

title: Binding Biometrics with AI Agent Identifiers for Delegation of Authority
summary: BIND binds a user's biometric data to an AI agent identifier and authority scope at authorization time using a fuzzy commitment over face features with turbo error-correcting codes, so an identity auditor can authenticate the user and recover the agent ID and scope, giving non-repudiable proof of human delegation; experiments report a 96% true match rate at zero false matches with 1024-bit agent tokens. The arXiv comment reports acceptance at IJCB 2026; no publisher record confirms it yet.
whyItMatters: A biometric route to the human-presence and delegation evidence that visa-tap consumer recognition and ap2 mandates rely on.

title: Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents against Prompt Injections
summary: Proposes a set of principled design patterns that restrict how untrusted inputs can influence an agent's actions, analyzes their utility and security trade-offs, and illustrates them with case studies of real applications.
whyItMatters: A practical checklist for anyone building a buying agent on ACP, AP2 or x402: the patterns constrain which parts of agent state untrusted merchant content may ever touch.

title: Bonded Recourse for Smart-Contract Settlement of Compensable Agent Side Effects
summary: Designs Recourse, a set of smart contracts that binds each agent action to its scope, recovery plan, evidence, payout and collateral, so residual harm from a permitted action that fails can be settled through an optimistic oracle or arbitration. The authors deploy it on Base Sepolia and report less uncompensated harm than authorization-only baselines; the arXiv comment says it was accepted at IEEE BCCA 2026, not yet confirmed in proceedings.
whyItMatters: Adds the after-the-fact remedy that payment and identity protocols lack; it pairs naturally with ERC-8004 reputation and on-chain settlement used by x402.

title: Macaroons: Cookies with Contextual Caveats for Decentralized Authorization in the Cloud
summary: Introduces macaroons, bearer credentials built from chained HMACs that any holder can attenuate by adding caveats (contextual restrictions such as time, target or third-party discharge) without contacting the issuer, enabling decentralized delegation in cloud services.
whyItMatters: The attenuable-token model behind later agent delegation designs (Biscuit tokens in AIP, scoped mandates in ap2) and a reference point for how visa-tap and openai-acp scope agent authority. AP2: Caveat-based attenuation, an ancestor of constraint-limited delegation. x402: Macaroons, the credential in the original L402 design (an earlier HTTP 402 approach on Lightning).

title: The next-generation monetary and financial system
venue: BIS Annual Economic Report 2025, chapter III
summary: Argues that tokenized platforms built around central bank reserves, commercial bank money and government bonds can form the next monetary system, and that stablecoins fail the three tests of singleness, elasticity and integrity needed to be its mainstay. Published 2025-06-29.
whyItMatters: x402 and the on-chain MPP methods settle mostly in stablecoins; this chapter is the leading central bank critique of that settlement asset.

title: Chip and Skim: Cloning EMV Cards with the Pre-play Attack
venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy 2014
summary: Finds that many EMV terminals and ATMs generate weak or predictable "unpredictable numbers", which lets an attacker who briefly accesses a card harvest authorization cryptograms in advance and replay them later as if the card were present (the pre-play attack).
whyItMatters: Replay of pre-computed authorizations is the same failure class that agent payment specs try to block with nonces, timestamps and per-request signatures, as in Visa TAP signatures and network tokens.

title: Agentic AI and Consumer Protection
summary: An issue paper (published 2026-07-16) asking whether EU consumer law, built on the assumption that a human makes the final purchase decision, is ready for AI shopping agents, and proposing how to adapt it. It is part of CERRE's Regulatory Lab series, which received input from members including Apple, Booking.com and Microsoft.
whyItMatters: Checkout protocols such as ACP and UCP assume the agent can confirm a purchase; this paper explains where EU disclosure and consent rules may not fit that flow. Agentic Commerce Protocol (ACP): Consumer protection analysis of agentic commerce including ACP.

title: IDs for AI Systems
summary: Proposes a framework in which IDs are ascribed to instances of AI systems, such as a particular agent session, with associated information accessible to parties that interact with them, and argues that demand for IDs is strongest where systems can make financial transactions or contact real people. The arXiv comment reports acceptance at the RegML workshop at NeurIPS 2024; no publisher record confirms it, so no venue is shown.
whyItMatters: Direct conceptual ancestor of per-agent identity in visa-tap, erc-8004 registrations and the agent credentials in ap2 mandates. Visa Trusted Agent Protocol: Agent identifiers, the general problem TAP solves for one network.

title: Visibility into AI Agents
summary: Assesses three measures for visibility into AI agents, agent identifiers, real-time monitoring and activity logging, outlines implementations that vary in intrusiveness and informativeness, and analyzes how they apply across centralized and decentralized deployments, including implications for privacy and concentration of power.
whyItMatters: Foundation for the agent identifier idea that visa-tap, erc-8004 and ap2 each implement in their own way.

title: Infrastructure for AI Agents
summary: Introduces the concept of agent infrastructure, technical systems and shared protocols external to agents that mediate their interactions, and identifies three functions: attributing actions and properties to agents and their principals, shaping agent interactions, and detecting and remedying harm. whyItMatters: The framing paper for treating x402, ap2, erc-8004 and the card-network protocols as infrastructure rather than model behavior. Visa Trusted Agent Protocol: Attribution and interaction infrastructure for agents, of which signed requests are one piece.

title: Agent Network Protocol Technical White Paper
summary: The technical white paper for the Agent Network Protocol (ANP), a community-led three-layer stack covering identity and encrypted communication, meta-protocol negotiation, and application-level capability description for agents on the open web. It is a reformatted version of the open-source community edition.
whyItMatters: ANP is a neighbor protocol in the atlas orbit: it handles agent identity and discovery with decentralized identifiers but has no payment layer, which shows where ERC-8004 and the payment protocols fit.

title: Reputation as Community Memory for the Agentic Web
summary: Presents Cairn, a community reputation platform in which agents query the collective opinion of a data source, service or tool before use and submit evidence-backed ratings afterward, aggregated by a time-decayed Beta model with confidence shrinkage and searchable by reviewer rationale. The engine is evaluated under lying, collusion and camouflage, and in a production case study rating heterogeneous agents.
whyItMatters: An off-chain alternative to ERC-8004's registry for the same question (should an agent trust this resource), useful as a design comparison for aggregation and adversarial robustness. ERC-8004: Trustless Agents: A design view of reputation as shared memory for agents.

title: Blind Signatures for Untraceable Payments
summary: Introduces blind signatures, where a signer signs a message without seeing it, and uses them to build payments that the bank can verify but cannot link back to the payer.
whyItMatters: The origin of private digital cash; it frames the privacy trade-off in agent payments, where x402 settles on public ledgers and card-based agent payments expose purchase data to the networks.

title: 2030 Forecast: How Agentic AI Will Reshape US Retail
summary: A short forecast (2025-12-17) estimating the US agentic commerce market at $300 billion to $500 billion by 2030, about 15% to 25% of e-commerce, with specification-driven purchases such as household essentials moving first.
whyItMatters: Another anchor for the forecast range used in the atlas market pages; Bain counts transactions that agents start, influence or complete.

title: terms.txt: A Consent and Compensation Protocol for Agentic Web Access
summary: Specifies terms.txt, a robots.txt-style file for per-path, per-purpose machine-access terms, and an origin-enforced exchange combining Web Bot Auth signatures, signed intent, delegation tokens, HTTP 402 negotiation and signed receipts, with a dependency-free implementation adding 0.20 to 0.65 ms per request. The arXiv comment reports submission to IEEE Internet Computing; it is not accepted as of the arXiv record.
whyItMatters: Combines the Web Bot Auth signatures that visa-tap builds on with HTTP 402 negotiation in the style of x402 and stripe-mpp, for content access rather than checkout.

title: Strabo: Declarative Specification and Implementation of Agentic Interaction Protocols
summary: Models the checkout part of Google's Universal Commerce Protocol as a declarative Langshaw interaction protocol, implements agents for it in the Peach programming model, and shows those agents interoperating with UCP agents built by Google. The arXiv comment says it was presented at the EMAS workshop at AAMAS 2026.
whyItMatters: One of only two papers found on 2026-10-11 that analyze UCP by name; it shows that UCP checkout can be specified declaratively and checked for interoperability. UCP: Models UCP checkout as a declarative protocol and reports interoperation with Google's UCP agents; one of two papers that name UCP.

title: Delegating Authorization to Misaligned Agents: Coalitional Alignment and Safe Control
summary: Studies when a principal can safely delegate approval of a long-running agent's actions to a panel of possibly misaligned reviewer agents, and characterizes k-robust coalitional alignment as the necessary and sufficient condition for a threshold approval rule to guarantee the principal does at least as well as a baseline policy, extending the result to sequential control in discounted MDPs and to strategic voting.
whyItMatters: Theory for the human-approval bottleneck that ap2 mandates and openai-acp checkout confirmations encode; it asks when approval itself can be delegated. AP2: Theory of approving actions of possibly misaligned agents.

title: opML: Optimistic Machine Learning on Blockchain
summary: Proposes opML, which runs machine learning inference for blockchains under an optimistic model: results are accepted unless a challenger wins an interactive fraud-proof game, similar to optimistic rollups. The authors argue this is far cheaper than zero-knowledge proofs and can serve large models on ordinary hardware.
whyItMatters: Shows the crypto-economic alternative to zkML for ERC-8004 validation, where validators stake on a result and disputes, not proofs, keep inference honest. ERC-8004: Trustless Agents: Optimistic re-execution, close to stake-secured validation.

title: Intel SGX Explained
summary: A long technical analysis of Intel Software Guard Extensions built from Intel papers, manuals, a tutorial and patents. It explains enclave creation, memory protection and remote attestation, and it catalogs the side-channel and design weaknesses that limit the trust these guarantees deserve.
whyItMatters: TEE attestation is one of the validation methods ERC-8004 anticipates; this paper is the standard reference for what an SGX attestation proves and where it does not hold. ERC-8004: Trustless Agents: Background on TEE attestation for validators.

title: How Agentic AI Will Reshape Payments
summary: Examines how agentic AI could change authorization, liquidity, settlement, compliance and resilience in payments, using a three-layer model of intent, authorization and settlement. It stresses the tension between probabilistic AI behavior and the deterministic requirements of payment systems.
whyItMatters: The IMF view of where agent decisions should stop and rule-based payment execution should begin, a split visible in how AP2 mandates and card network tokens separate intent from settlement.

Visa Trusted Agent Protocol: Privacy Pass, a CDN-world alternative for telling clients apart without identifying them.

title: AgentDojo: A Dynamic Environment to Evaluate Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses for LLM Agents
summary: An extensible environment for agents that run tools over untrusted data, with 97 realistic tasks (email, e-banking, travel booking), 629 security test cases and pluggable attacks and defenses. Frontier models fail many tasks even without attacks, and existing injections break some but not all security properties.
whyItMatters: Its e-banking and booking suites are the closest public testbed to agent payments, and the defenses cited here (CaMeL, multi-CaMeL) report their numbers on it.

title: Defeating Prompt Injections by Design
venue: IEEE Conference on Secure and Trustworthy Machine Learning (SaTML 2026), pp. 587-618
summary: CaMeL wraps the LLM in a protective system layer that extracts control and data flow from the trusted user query, so retrieved data can never alter program flow, and attaches capabilities to values so tool calls are checked against security policies. It solved 77 percent of AgentDojo tasks with provable security versus 84 percent for an undefended agent.
whyItMatters: The capability model is a natural enforcement point for payment policy: an AP2 cart mandate or an x402 spend limit can be expressed as a CaMeL policy on the payment tool's arguments.

title: RAILS: Verification-Native Clearing For Agentic Commerce
summary: Defines the agentic clearing problem, deciding whether an agent met its delegated obligation and which settlement action follows, and argues that MCP, A2A, x402, AP2 and the Visa and Mastercard network agent protocols all assume that determination without producing it. RAILS specifies seven primitives and a formal model of admissibility-graded verification yielding a soundness property that no financially material settlement rests on evidence below the obligation's admissibility floor. The abstract names Visa and Mastercard generically rather than by protocol name.
whyItMatters: Names x402, ap2 and the Visa and Mastercard agent programs as rails that lack a clearing layer; useful for the atlas comparison of where disputes and fulfillment evidence live. Visa Trusted Agent Protocol: The only paper found that names TAP; places it as the network's edge attestation layer.

title: From Product Search to Preference Articulation: The Economics of Agentic Commerce
summary: A search-theoretic model that compares manual product search, which evaluates a few products accurately, with agentic search, which screens a broad catalog through noisy representations of preferences. Manual search collapses beyond a preference-complexity threshold and platform revenue falls to zero, while agentic search avoids the collapse; the paper derives how platforms should set agent refinement depth.
whyItMatters: Supplies the economic rationale for the discovery and product-feed layers of UCP and OpenAI ACP: once consumers delegate search, platform revenue depends on how well the agent elicits preferences rather than on how many items a person inspects. UCP: Economics of agentic commerce, from product search to preference articulation.

title: The Sybil Attack
venue: IPTPS 2002 (1st International Workshop on Peer-to-Peer Systems), Lecture Notes in Computer Science, Springer, pp. 251-260
summary: Shows that in a large peer-to-peer system without a logically centralized authority, a single faulty entity can present many identities and defeat the redundancy the system relies on, and that such Sybil attacks remain possible except under unrealistic assumptions of resource parity and coordination among entities.
whyItMatters: Defines the attack every permissionless agent registry inherits: ERC-8004 identities and feedback without a trusted issuer are exposed to it, which is why TAP and the card networks keep a certifying authority in the loop. ERC-8004: Trustless Agents: The original Sybil attack result behind the reviewer-filter design.

title: LEGIT: Credentialing Protocol for Trustworthy AI Agent Marketplaces
summary: A credentialing protocol that binds measured quality and cost per solved task to a signed record of agent configuration, task domain, evaluation budget and evidence, links past outcomes to the same identity as reputation, and lets buyers verify the records. Evaluations show that agents with similar success differ in cost and that comparisons depend on budget; a complementary analysis prices the deposits and fees needed to manipulate reputation under a stated Sybil model.
whyItMatters: A concrete alternative design for the certification and feedback roles that ERC-8004's Validation and Reputation registries describe, with explicit Sybil cost accounting.

title: A survey of agent interoperability protocols: Model Context Protocol (MCP), Agent Communication Protocol (ACP), Agent-to-Agent Protocol (A2A), and Agent Network Protocol (ANP)
summary: Compares MCP, IBM's Agent Communication Protocol, Google's A2A and the Agent Network Protocol on interaction modes, discovery, communication patterns and security models, and proposes a phased adoption roadmap that ends with ANP for decentralized agent marketplaces.
whyItMatters: Background for the transport layer under the commerce protocols, with one caution: its ACP is IBM's Agent Communication Protocol, not OpenAI's Agentic Commerce Protocol, so the acronym must not be conflated.

title: WASP: Benchmarking Web Agent Security Against Prompt Injection Attacks
summary: An end-to-end benchmark for web agents facing realistic, low-effort human-written injections in tasks such as paying bills. Even top reasoning models were partially deceived in up to 86 percent of cases yet rarely completed the attacker's full goal, which the authors call security by incompetence.
whyItMatters: Web agents that pay bills are the use case TAP and AP2 target; WASP's finding that attacks succeed partially but not fully is a warning that capability gains will remove the accidental protection.

title: Agentic Commerce World: An Auditable and Verifiable Environment for Vibe Commerce
summary: ACWorld is an environment in which independently controlled buyer and merchant agents transact through a Vibe Commerce Protocol that validates each action before updating shared state and records the interactions for audit. Its benchmark has a 200-task capability track and a 60-task large-catalog track over 785,022 listings; ten models score 65.9 to 85.6 percent and 56.1 to 91.4 percent, and process-level evidence catches errors that final state misses.
whyItMatters: A reproducible testbed for the buyer-agent to merchant-agent transaction loop that OpenAI ACP and UCP standardize, with an audit-log design relevant to dispute handling.

title: Notarized Agents: Receiver-Attested Confidential Receipts for AI Agent Actions
summary: Proposes receiver-attested receipts for agent actions: the service receiving an agent's call signs a receipt of what it observed, encrypts it to the agent's owner (bound to the authorization token through JWS) and publishes it to a witness-cosigned transparency log, so the owner can reconstruct a tamper-evident trail without trusting the agent or its operator. Instantiated as Sello, with microbenchmarks and a discussion of suppression and collusion attacks.
whyItMatters: An audit primitive for delegated agent actions that would complement the merchant-side evidence in ap2 and openai-acp flows.

title: Tempting the Agent: The Economics of Reputation without Persistent Identity in AI Agent Markets
summary: A dynamic model in which an agent's reputation is capital that attracts future demand, and the agent chooses each period between honest operation, investing in quality, or a one-shot deviation that cashes out the reputation and restarts under a penalized new identity. The temptation depends on identity-reset cost, reputation persistence, demand sensitivity and enforcement design; ERC-8004, ERC-8183 and x402 are named as the motivating infrastructure.
whyItMatters: Names ERC-8004 and x402 directly and states the economic condition under which an on-chain reputation registry disciplines agents: resetting an identity must cost more than the one-shot gain from burning it. ERC-8004: Trustless Agents: Economics of reputation when identities are cheap.

title: The Millicent Protocol for Inexpensive Electronic Commerce
venue: Fourth International World Wide Web Conference (WWW4)
summary: Describes Millicent, a protocol for web purchases below one cent in which brokers sell vendor-specific scrip that each vendor can validate locally, without extra network round trips or heavy cryptography. Brokers handle accounts and billing so vendors and customers do not need direct financial relationships.
whyItMatters: The direct ancestor of pay-per-request web payments: x402 and MPP revisit the same goal of charging tiny amounts per HTTP resource, with stablecoins and facilitators in the broker role.

title: Agentic AI in Payments: Establishing Interoperable Trust and Control
summary: A working paper (cover dated September 2026, written by contributors from GLEIF, Curvy Protocol, zERC20, Terminal 3 and an independent expert) arguing that existing law can allocate liability for agent payments but practical proof of delegated authority is missing. It proposes Agent Mandate Credentials anchored in the verifiable LEI to show which organization stands behind an agent and what it may do.
whyItMatters: Offers an organizational-identity answer to the "who is behind this agent" question that ERC-8004 registries, Visa TAP keys and Agent Pay tokens each answer differently.

title: TessIndex: Capability Verified Identity System for the Agent Economy
summary: Proposes TessIndex, an agent identity system that records compact identity, ownership and verification commitments on a blockchain while keeping discovery, commerce and reputation metadata on servers, and replaces self-declared capabilities with predicate-based capability proofs. It comes from the same authors as TessPay.
whyItMatters: A close design alternative to the ERC-8004 identity and validation registries, with the same split between on-chain anchors and off-chain metadata.

title: TessPay: Verify-then-Pay Infrastructure for Trusted Agentic Commerce
summary: Introduces TessPay, a two-plane verify-then-pay infrastructure for agentic commerce: agents are anchored in a canonical registry and user intent is captured as verifiable mandates, funds are escrowed during execution while the agent produces cryptographic evidence (TLS Notary, TEE) for a Proof of Task Execution, settlement releases funds only when the evidence satisfies verification predicates, and a tamper-evident audit trail supports disputes.
whyItMatters: Combines the mandate idea of ap2 with the registry and validation functions of erc-8004 into one escrow design; a useful comparison for how the protocols split those functions.

title: Agent-to-Agent Finance: Blockchain Payments and Trust Infrastructure for Autonomous AI Agents
summary: A chapter-length treatment of agent-to-agent finance as a layer of machine-mediated financial interaction in which agents discover counterparties, express intent, pay and generate auditable evidence, drawing on blockchain agent-to-agent payment work, ERC-8004 registries, provenance-based wallets and official evidence on AI adoption in finance. Its central design question is bounded autonomy.
whyItMatters: Positions erc-8004 and blockchain agent payments such as x402 as candidate financial market infrastructure and sets out the accountability questions regulators will ask.

title: Authority-Inference Separation in Agentic Finance: First-Line Control, Blockchain Enforcement, and Replayable Assurance
summary: Develops Authority-Inference Separation, an architecture in which an agent's proposed financial action gains temporary executable authority only after a deterministic control plane validates registered identity, accountable ownership, mandate lineage, policy version and exact economic semantics, with blockchain enforcing granted authority and recording evidence. A 48-fixture prototype rejected all 36 synthetic authorization attacks, and a test of 1,700 Base transactions tied to public x402 facilitator addresses shows that public ledgers evidence settlement but not mandate, accountability or delivery.
whyItMatters: Uses live x402 facilitator traffic to show what on-chain data cannot prove, and frames mandate lineage in terms that map onto ap2 mandates and erc-8004 identity.

title: Agentic JWT: A Secure Delegation Protocol for Autonomous AI Agents
summary: Introduces Agentic JWT, an intent token that binds each agent action to verifiable user intent and optionally to a workflow step, carrying an agent identity hash derived from prompt, tools and configuration, a chained delegation assertion and per-agent proof-of-possession keys, with a Python proof of concept that blocks scope violations, replay, impersonation and prompt-injection paths.
whyItMatters: An OAuth-aligned intent token that parallels the mandate concept in ap2 and the agent identity assertions in visa-tap.

title: Not What You've Signed Up For: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection
venue: AISec 2023 (16th ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security, at CCS 2023), pp. 79-90
summary: Introduces indirect prompt injection: adversaries plant instructions in data that an LLM-integrated application will retrieve, so the model is attacked without any direct interface. The paper gives a security taxonomy of impacts, including data theft, worming and contamination of the information ecosystem, and demonstrates attacks on real systems.
whyItMatters: The founding paper for the threat every agentic payment protocol must contain; AP2 mandates, x402 pre-execution filters, TAP intent signatures and ACP's structured checkout all exist partly because retrieved merchant content can hijack the buying agent. Agentic Commerce Protocol (ACP): Indirect prompt injection, relevant to merchant text rendered by the agent.

title: VET Your Agent: Towards Host-Independent Autonomy via Verifiable Execution Traces
summary: Introduces Verifiable Execution Traces, a compositional framework for host-independent authentication of agent outputs built on an Agent Identity Document that specifies configuration and proof systems, supporting trusted hardware, succinct proofs and notarized TLS transcripts; for secret-bearing API calls Web Proofs add under 3x overhead, and a verifiable trading agent is deployed as a case study.
whyItMatters: Provides the kind of attestation evidence that the erc-8004 Validation Registry is designed to record and that TessPay-style escrow would consume.

title: An Economy of AI Agents
summary: A survey chapter for economists on how AI agents that plan and act over long horizons with little oversight might interact with people and with each other, reshape markets and organizations, and what institutions would be needed for such markets to work.
whyItMatters: Frames the institutional questions (identity, liability, enforcement) that ERC-8004 registries and AP2 mandates try to answer with technical artifacts.

title: Multi-Agent Risks from Advanced AI
summary: A Cooperative AI Foundation technical report that sorts risks from interacting AI agents into three failure modes (miscoordination, conflict and collusion) and seven risk factors such as information asymmetry, network effects and commitment problems.
whyItMatters: Agent-to-agent commerce is a multi-agent system; the taxonomy names the market failures, such as collusion between buyer and seller agents, that payment protocols alone cannot prevent.

title: Accountable yet Anonymous AI Agents - Split-Knowledge Binding in National Agent-Identity Layer in China
summary: Documents a national agent-identity system in China, scheduled for public launch in Q3 2026, in which an agent is bound to a verified legal principal that is not disclosed to business-layer participants and can be re-identified only by compelling two separate government agencies, a mechanism the authors call split-knowledge binding and describe as institutional rather than cryptographic. The paper is a pre-launch v1 and promises post-launch measurements.
whyItMatters: A state-run alternative to erc-8004 style permissionless identity and to network-issued agent identity in visa-tap and mastercard-agent-pay; status is announced, not yet measured.

title: The User Asks, Platforms Compete: How Agentic Recommendation Markets Take Shape
summary: Studies agentic recommendation markets in which a user agent states a need first and platforms compete for its attention. Across three product domains, broader access does not translate into exposure, platforms answer with selectively positive explanations in 73 to 78 percent of first-ranked positions, and tying platform behavior to later user feedback cuts this to 36 to 41 percent while raising purchases of the relevant item.
whyItMatters: Models the merchant-side incentives that UCP and ACP discovery surfaces create when many sellers answer one agent's query, and argues that access, attention and accountability must be designed as one mechanism. Agentic Commerce Protocol (ACP): Platform competition in agentic recommendation, context for ranking and fees. UCP: Economics of agentic recommendation markets and platform competition.

title: Inter-Agent Trust Models: A Comparative Study of Brief, Claim, Proof, Stake, Reputation and Constraint in Agentic Web Protocol Design-A2A, AP2, ERC-8004, and Beyond
summary: Compares six trust mechanisms for inter-agent protocols (brief, claim, proof, stake, reputation, constraint) and evaluates A2A, AP2 and ERC-8004 against them on security, privacy, cost and resistance to Sybil, collusion and whitewashing, with attention to LLM-specific weaknesses such as prompt injection and sycophancy. It argues that proof and stake should gate high-impact actions, with claims for discovery and reputation as an overlay. The arXiv record says it was submitted to the AAAI 2026 TrustAgent workshop; acceptance is not confirmed.
whyItMatters: Direct comparative treatment of ap2 and erc-8004 trust assumptions; its warning that claim-only and reputation-only designs are brittle anticipates the empirical ERC-8004 Sybil findings. ERC-8004: Trustless Agents: Places ERC-8004 reputation among other inter-agent trust models.

title: Dissociative Identity: Language Model Agents Lack Grounding for Reputation Mechanisms
venue: ACM FAccT 2026 (Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency), pp. 4199-4219
summary: Argues that Know Your Agent regimes modeled on human identity verification and credit scores are incomplete because language model agents are assemblages of mutable modules (models, prompts, tool policies, memory) with fluid personas that may not internalize sanctions, so identifiability, predictability, credibility and rehabilitability lack grounding. It proposes observability-based, ex ante, protocol-level behavioral harnesses in place of ex post reputation.
whyItMatters: A direct critique of the premise behind ERC-8004's Reputation Registry and of KYA-style identity checks in TAP and Agent Pay: if the sanctioned identity can be swapped out, reputation does not discipline the agent. ERC-8004: Trustless Agents: Questions whether LLM agents have the stable identity reputation needs.

title: Agent Name Service (ANS): A Universal Directory for Secure AI Agent Discovery and Interoperability
summary: Proposes the Agent Name Service, a DNS-inspired, protocol-agnostic registry that uses PKI certificates for verifiable agent identity, with a registration and renewal lifecycle, capability-aware naming and resolution, and a protocol adapter layer for A2A, MCP and others, accompanied by JSON Schema definitions and a threat analysis.
whyItMatters: A PKI-based alternative to the erc-8004 Identity Registry for agent discovery.

title: A Novel Zero-Trust Identity Framework for Agentic AI: Decentralized Authentication and Fine-Grained Access Control
summary: Argues that OAuth, OIDC and SAML style IAM is inadequate for ephemeral, interdependent AI agents and proposes a framework built on verifiable agent identities using DIDs and VCs, an Agent Naming Service for discovery, fine-grained dynamic access control, a global session and policy enforcement layer for revocation, and zero-knowledge proofs for selective disclosure.
whyItMatters: A frequently cited zero-trust identity blueprint that overlaps with the discovery and identity roles of erc-8004 and the agent recognition goals of visa-tap. Visa Trusted Agent Protocol: A decentralized alternative to a network-controlled agent identity.

title: Capability-Priced Micro-Markets: A Micro-Economic Framework for the Agentic Web over HTTP 402
summary: Introduces Capability-Priced Micro-Markets, combining Project NANDA capability-based discovery, HTTP 402 micropayments with x402 and H402 extensions, and the Agent Capability Negotiation and Binding Protocol into a repeated bilateral game with incomplete information, shown to converge to a constrained Radner equilibrium, and defines a privacy elasticity of demand.
whyItMatters: A micro-economic model of markets priced over x402-style HTTP 402 payments.

title: The Verifiable Action Card: Trustworthy Human-in-the-Loop Control for Secure Autonomous Agents
summary: Proposes the Verifiable Action Card, which rebuilds the confirmation prompt in an agentic browser from the action that will actually execute, shows it in trusted browser chrome and binds approval to that exact action at dispatch. On a 24-scenario benchmark it cuts attack success from 68% to 100% down to 0% across the tested models.
whyItMatters: Human confirmation is the step-up that card agent programs and AP2 rely on for higher-risk purchases; this shows how that confirmation can be forged and one way to bind it to the real transaction.

title: A Formal Analysis of Agent Payment Protocols
summary: Builds Tamarin models of x402, MPP, ACP and AP2 from their specifications, schemas and reference code using one shared abstraction of the agent payment lifecycle, then asks source-backed verification questions to expose missing bindings and cross-stage correspondences, which it consolidates into 18 security principles. Across 86 verification cases it reproduces 46 known or calibration cases, reports 40 new formal-consistency findings, and validates ten of them against x402 implementations with proofs of concept.
whyItMatters: The only side-by-side formal model of x402, stripe-mpp, openai-acp and ap2 so far; it shows where each specification leaves delegated authority, settlement and fulfillment unbound. AP2: Tamarin models that include AP2. ERC-8004: Trustless Agents: Formal models of agent payment protocols around ERC-8004. Agentic Commerce Protocol (ACP): Models ACP in Tamarin with x402, MPP and AP2; the only formal analysis that names it. UCP: Formal analysis of agent payment protocols; the abstract does not name UCP but analyzes AP2, which UCP embeds as an extension. x402: Formal Tamarin models of x402 alongside MPP, ACP and AP2.

title: The Web4 Agent Economy: A Large-Scale Empirical Study of the Landscape, Challenges, and Opportunities
summary: Large-scale empirical study of the Web4 agent economy built on MCP, x402 and EIP-8004 (ERC-8004), analyzing 99,448 multi-chain identity registrations, 317,596,323 transaction logs, the source code of 341 MCP projects and 349 GitHub issues. It finds a highly active machine-to-machine payment economy with millions of daily transactions resting on immature identity, authorization and interoperability practice, with payment interoperability the most persistent bottleneck.
whyItMatters: Measurement of erc-8004 registrations and x402 transaction volume from a software-engineering angle; read it together with the authenticity analyses before quoting volume figures.

title: A Survey of Trust and Reputation Systems for Online Service Provision
venue: Decision Support Systems, vol. 43, no. 2, pp. 618-644
summary: Surveys systems in which parties rate each other after transactions and aggregated ratings guide future decisions, describing them as collaborative sanctioning systems that also create an incentive for good behavior. It reviews commercial and proposed designs, analyzes trends and proposes a research agenda.
whyItMatters: The reference taxonomy for reputation computation that ERC-8004 reputation clients and off-chain scorers draw on, and a reminder that the field predates agents by two decades. ERC-8004: Trustless Agents: Survey of trust and reputation systems.

title: The EigenTrust Algorithm for Reputation Management in P2P Networks
venue: WWW 2003 (12th International World Wide Web Conference)
summary: Assigns each peer a single global trust value computed by power iteration over local trust ratings, in a distributed and secure way, so peers can avoid downloading inauthentic files. Simulations show the system isolates malicious peers even when they collude.
whyItMatters: The standard reference for turning pairwise feedback, such as the entries ERC-8004's Reputation Registry stores, into a global score, and for the collusion cases any such aggregator must resist.

title: Scaling up Trustless DNN Inference with Zero-Knowledge Proofs
summary: Builds the first ZK-SNARK proof of correct inference for a full-resolution ImageNet model, so a client can check after the fact that a machine learning service ran the promised model. It also sketches protocols that use these proofs to verify model accuracy and to pay for verified predictions.
whyItMatters: An early, concrete answer to the question an ERC-8004 validator asks: did the service actually run the model it claimed, and can that be checked without trusting the server. ERC-8004: Trustless Agents: Zero-knowledge inference, another validation path.

title: Governance Gaps in Agent Interoperability Protocols: What MCP, A2A, and ACP Cannot Express
summary: Applies a six-dimension governance taxonomy (membership, deliberation, voting, dissent preservation, human escalation, audit and replay) to the specifications of MCP, A2A, ACP, ANP and ERC-8004, finding that voting and dissent preservation are absent in all five and that governed agent communities need a new architectural layer above interoperability standards. The ACP it analyzes is an agent interoperability protocol, not OpenAI's Agentic Commerce Protocol; its exact referent is not confirmed from the abstract.
whyItMatters: One of the few papers to read the erc-8004 specification text against a requirements taxonomy; it also illustrates the ACP name clash.

title: Governing AI Agents
summary: Uses the economics of principal-agent problems and the common law of agency to analyze AI agents, identifying problems of information asymmetry, discretionary authority and loyalty, and argues that incentives, monitoring and enforcement work poorly for agents acting at machine speed and scale.
whyItMatters: Frames delegated purchasing in legal terms, which matters for the mandate and consent records that AP2, Agent Pay and the other protocols produce as evidence of authority. AP2: Legal and governance frame for agents acting for principals.

title: Zero-Trust Runtime Verification for Agentic Payment Protocols: Mitigating Replay and Context-Binding Failures in AP2
summary: Analyzes the AP2 mandate lifecycle and finds runtime enforcement gaps created by retries, concurrency and orchestration, then proposes a zero-trust runtime verifier that enforces explicit context binding and consume-once mandate semantics with time-bound nonces. Simulations at up to 10,000 transactions per second show both mechanisms are needed to stop replay and context-redirect attacks, at about 3.8 ms verification latency.
whyItMatters: Shows that ap2 (and ucp, which it also names as a mandate-based protocol) needs execution-time checks on mandates, not just signature validity at issuance. AP2: Replay and context-binding gaps in the mandate lifecycle. UCP: Names UCP and AP2 in its abstract; replay and context-binding failures in mandate-based protocols.

title: NostrAgent: A Decentralized Identity and Delegation Architecture for Sovereign Agentic Systems
summary: Unifies persistent identity, scoped delegation, peer trust, discovery and payment over Nostr relays with three custom event kinds (identity declarations with BIP340 Schnorr signatures and pre-rotation commitments, scoped delegation chains that narrow at each hop, and peer attestations forming a Sybil-deterrent trust graph), with Lightning L402 payments bound to agent identity. A Python prototype shows sub-millisecond offline verification and 157 ms median L402 settlement on regtest. The arXiv comment reports acceptance at AGENTICS 2026 (IJCCI 2026) for Springer CCIS; no publisher record confirms it yet.
whyItMatters: A registry-free alternative to erc-8004 identity and reputation, paired with L402, the Lightning cousin of x402.

title: Commercial LLM Agents Are Already Vulnerable to Simple Yet Dangerous Attacks
summary: Provides a taxonomy of attacks specific to agent pipelines, organized by threat actor, objective, entry point, attacker observability, strategy and inherent pipeline weaknesses, and demonstrates simple, practical attacks on popular open-source and commercial agents.
whyItMatters: Documents that deployed browsing and shopping agents, the clients that ACP and UCP checkouts serve, can be steered by web content without any model jailbreak.

title: 402Pilot: An x402 Decision Layer for Autonomous Agent Micropayments
summary: Frames the buyer side of x402 as a decision problem, selecting among payable providers under a finite wallet with feedback only on chosen purchases, and proposes 402Pilot, a protocol-agnostic decision layer instantiated with a payment-aware discounted contextual Thompson-sampling policy. On the 402Pilot-Bench replay benchmark (823 tasks, five provider pipelines, three market regimes) it keeps service quality while spending 39 to 43 percent of the wallet.
whyItMatters: Treats x402 as settled infrastructure and asks how an agent should decide what to buy over it; a bridge between the payment rail and agent economics. x402: A decision layer for when an agent should pay an x402 price.

title: A402: Binding Cryptocurrency Payments to Service Execution for Agentic Commerce
summary: Proposes A402, a payment architecture that binds cryptocurrency payments to service execution through Atomic Service Channels and TEE-assisted adaptor signatures, so that payment finalizes only if the requested service is executed and delivered, with a TEE-based liquidity vault aggregating channel settlements on chain. Evaluated against x402 on Bitcoin and Ethereum integrations.
whyItMatters: Addresses the end-to-end atomicity gap that x402 leaves open, and connects agent micropayments to the payment-channel lineage. x402: Shows that x402 does not bind payment to service execution and proposes Atomic Service Channels.

title: Five Attacks on x402 Agentic Payment Protocol
summary: Formalizes x402 and demonstrates five practical attacks on authorization, binding, replay protection and web-layer handling, validated on local chains, Base Sepolia and live endpoints, plus an audit of three open-source SDKs and endpoints. The attacks yield either unpaid service or paid-but-denied outcomes, and the paper proposes mitigations.
whyItMatters: Direct attack catalog for x402 that spans the HTTP layer and the on-chain settlement layer. x402: Five practical attacks and an audit of three x402 SDKs; the main source for section H.

title: Emergent Misaligned Communication in Long-Horizon Multi-Agent LLM Commerce
summary: Analyzes 2,583 inter-agent emails from twenty one-year runs of Vending-Bench Arena across 13 frontier models and labels 12.6 percent as misaligned (false factual claims, manipulation, collusion or threats). Misalignment appears in every run and in 74.7 percent of agent-runs, is reciprocal, rises under inventory scarcity, and is not predicted by model capability rank.
whyItMatters: Agent-to-agent commerce protocols assume counterparties negotiate in good faith; this measurement shows deceptive speech acts emerging without adversarial prompting, which bears on reputation layers in ERC-8004 and on merchant-agent trust in ACP and UCP.

title: A Finger on the Scale: Covert Policy Steering through Agentic Skills
summary: Treats reusable agent skills as externalized policies and presents SkillShift, a supply-chain attack that keeps a skill's declared task and output interface while covertly steering decisions toward an undisclosed objective. In agentic commerce and dependency selection it achieved attacker-favored selection rates of 81.33 and 63.33 percent with no utility loss, transferred across backends, and evaded the evaluated scanners.
whyItMatters: A merchant-steering attack that needs no prompt injection: a shopping agent's skill package can bias which seller wins an ACP or UCP checkout while every protocol message stays valid.

title: Free-Riding the Agentic Web: A Systematic Security Analysis of x402 Payments
summary: Analyzes x402 as a stack of HTTP semantics, per-chain schemes and SDK choices against five invariants and finds four flaw classes: cross-resource substitution, duplicate-settlement races, allowance overdraft and denial of settlement, reaching resource-leakage ratios up to 100% against official SDKs and a production deployment. It also proves that output-only pay-per-token pricing cannot be both fair and bounded against hidden reasoning-token inflation, and proposes mitigations with provable guarantees.
whyItMatters: Explains the state-synchronization gap between synchronous HTTP and asynchronous settlement that is specific to x402-style rails. x402: Four flaw classes, including cross-resource substitution and a duplicate settlement race.

title: How Agentic Is Agentic Commerce? A Population-Scale Measurement of x402 Adoption and Authenticity
summary: Population-scale measurement of x402 on Base over a 280-day window (136,708,672 settlements worth about 44.1 million dollars) with a coarser Solana census. Resolving the true payer through the meta-transaction layer, the authors classify 21.20% of settlements as fictitious and 63.78% as internal to a linked cluster, bound genuinely independent value between about 188 thousand and 20.3 million dollars, and conclude that the settlement count measures manufacturability rather than adoption.
whyItMatters: The main source for the dispute over x402 volume authenticity; any x402 metric on the atlas should be shown alongside this analysis. x402: Population-scale measurement that questions x402 volume figures.

title: Markets, Not Planners: Decentralized Orchestration of LLM Agents with Private Information
summary: Replaces centralized orchestration with AgentLance, a repeated labor market in which agents bid on tasks using private costs, an allocator picks winners from bids and public reputation records, a VCG-style rule sets payments, and winners can subcontract through the same mechanism. It outperforms single-model, centralized and market baselines, and the authors show a centralized LLM allocator can be swayed by a single inserted preference.
whyItMatters: Demonstrates reputation records and payments working together to allocate agent labor, which is the combination ERC-8004 (reputation) and x402 (payment) aim to provide on open rails.

title: Attesting Outputs and Delegation Ancestry in Multi-Agent AI Systems
summary: Designs deployer-side attestations so that, after an incident in a multi-agent workflow, a verifier can tell which deployer released given output bytes and whether each cross-deployer delegation was authorized. It compares a signed linked list, a Merkle chain and a co-signed DAG, and only the co-signed DAG rejects a forged parent link after a child key is compromised.
whyItMatters: Gives the evidence model that ERC-8004 validation records and AP2 mandate chains need when work and authority pass through several agents operated by different parties.

title: A dataset of early blockchain-registered AI agents on Ethereum
summary: Describes a structured dataset of 10,000 ERC-8004 agents registered on Ethereum mainnet within a defined block range, combining on-chain identity records, minting and transfer events, reputation summaries and feedback records with resolved off-chain metadata, collected through Web3 RPC queries. The companion data are deposited on Harvard Dataverse under DOI 10.7910/DVN/HJZW8Q (a dataset DOI, which the arXiv record lists in place of a paper DOI).
whyItMatters: A reusable baseline for erc-8004 measurement work; the Mafrur and Khusumanegara readiness study builds on data of this kind. ERC-8004: Trustless Agents: A dataset of early Ethereum registrations for your own analysis.

title: Cryptographically verifiable authorization for autonomous AI agents: a falsifiable hypothesis and proof of concept
summary: Hypothesizes that agent authorization can be expressed as a cryptographically verifiable relation binding an agent principal, a concrete request, an execution context and policy satisfaction while keeping private attributes confidential, defines candidate properties (authorization soundness, principal, request and policy binding, replay resistance), and provides a Groth16 zk-SNARK proof of concept. Full author names are taken from the Frontiers DOI record; arXiv lists initials.
whyItMatters: Peer-reviewed formalization of the identity, request and execution binding that ap2 mandates approximate and that erc-8004 validation could attest.

title: A2ABreak: Systematic Security Analysis of the A2A Protocol
summary: Extracts a verified finite-state machine (37 states and 76 transitions from 929 formalized statements) from the A2A specification with LLM assistance and reasons over it to find 11 protocol-level vulnerabilities exploitable by specification-compliant adversaries, including cross-client context injection, credential harvesting through identity loss in multi-hop delegation chains, and exfiltration through unattested capability claims.
whyItMatters: ap2 and the a2a-x402 extension are layered on A2A, so specification-level flaws in A2A delegation and identity flow directly into their trust assumptions.

title: Protocol-Level Attacks on Agentic Commerce Platforms: A Cross-Platform Taxonomy, AIP-Bench, and Unified Defense
summary: Argues that the most consequential risks in agentic commerce platforms sit in the protocol between agents and commerce services rather than in the model, documenting 33 structural vulnerabilities across three platforms that succeed deterministically regardless of model, three of which chain into a payment hijack. Contributes a taxonomy, AIP-Bench as a deterministic benchmark, and PCAT, a platform-agnostic defense that removes four of five structural attack classes.
whyItMatters: Cross-platform evidence that protocol design, not model alignment, decides the security of openai-acp, ap2 and ucp style checkout flows; the three platforms are not named in the abstract, so the mapping is unconfirmed. Agentic Commerce Protocol (ACP): Protocol-level attacks on agentic commerce platforms; does not name ACP but covers the same layer. UCP: Cross-platform attack taxonomy for agentic commerce platforms; context for section H.

title: Signing the Transaction but Not the Decision: Whisper Attacks and a Binding Defense for AP2
summary: Shows that AP2 signs completed transactions but not the decisions leading to them, so ordinary product-description text can steer a shopping agent into fetching another user's payment credentials, assembling a valid cart that differs from what the user saw, or upgrading to a more expensive item, with success rates of 90%, 56% and 73.3% on the Gemini Flash-Lite models that AP2 sample agents use. Proposes A-VIP, a protocol-layer defense that binds credential lookups and cart lines to the session and listing, and releases AP2-WhisperBench with 1,544 scenarios.
whyItMatters: Direct follow-up to the whisper attacks on ap2 with a protocol-layer defense and a benchmark; it sharpens the point that mandate signatures do not cover intent formation. AP2: Shows mandates sign the transaction but not the decision; proposes a binding defense.

title: From Agent Identity to Agent Economy: Measuring the Operational Readiness of ERC-8004 AI Agents
venue: Journal of FinTech and Digital Assets, vol. 1, no. 2, pp. 69-88
summary: Asks whether ERC-8004 agents on Ethereum are operationally ready beyond registration by building an agent-level feature table (identity status, metadata, service declarations, reputation feedback, transfers, cross-chain registration) and an evidence-layer readiness framework, complemented by network analysis of owner-agent, feedback-client and wallet-transfer graphs. Early adoption is registration-heavy but operationally shallow, and ownership and feedback activity are concentrated in a few wallets and clients.
whyItMatters: Independent, journal-published measurement that supports the atlas distinction between erc-8004 identity registrations and a working agent economy. ERC-8004: Trustless Agents: Measures operational readiness of registered agents.

title: SoK: Security of Autonomous LLM Agents in Agentic Commerce
summary: A systematization of knowledge that frames the security of autonomous LLM agents in commerce along five dimensions (agent integrity, transaction authorization, inter-agent trust, market manipulation, regulatory compliance), derives 12 cross-layer attack vectors from a curated corpus of papers, protocol documents, industry reports and incidents, and proposes a layered defense for the authorization gaps in current agent payment protocols. The ACP it lists is written 'Agent Commerce Protocol', which may not be OpenAI's Agentic Commerce Protocol; that mapping is unconfirmed.
whyItMatters: Places erc-8004, ap2, x402 and stripe-mpp in one threat framework and argues that their authorization gaps compound across the reasoning, tooling, custody and settlement layers. AP2: Places AP2 among agent commerce attack vectors. x402: Security SoK of agentic commerce that covers x402.

title: HTTP Message Signatures for automated traffic
venue: IETF Internet-Draft draft-ietf-webbotauth-httpsig-protocol-00 (Web Bot Auth working group)
summary: The first Web Bot Auth working group draft (revision 00, 2026-09-01) for identifying automated HTTP clients with HTTP Message Signatures. It defines the Signature-Agent header for in-band key discovery, a JWKS-based key directory format and a well-known URI for serving it.
whyItMatters: The Visa TAP spec calls itself aligned with Web Bot Auth, Cloudflare says the Visa and Mastercard agent protocols build on it, and UCP offers an optional Web Bot Auth profile; this working group draft, posted almost a year after TAP launched, is the standards-track form of that request signing. Visa Trusted Agent Protocol: The IETF working group draft TAP is compared against.

title: Sprites and State Channels: Payment Networks that Go Faster than Lightning
summary: Proposes Sprites, a payment channel construction for smart-contract chains that cuts the worst-case time collateral is locked along a multi-hop route and supports partial deposits and withdrawals without closing the channel. It also gives a modular treatment of general state channels.
whyItMatters: A key reference for channel designs on Ethereum-style chains, where x402 settles; it explains the collateral and dispute costs any channel-based agent payment scheme must budget for.

title: Agentic Settlement Protocol: An Application Profile for Refundable, Delayed-Fulfilment Agent Commerce on Stablecoin Rails
summary: Proposes the Agentic Settlement Protocol, an application profile over on-chain authorize-and-capture escrow for purchases whose fulfillment is confirmed off-chain, with a three-deadline hold model, a fulfillment-verification ladder, engine-authoritative partial refunds with per-seller exposure controls, and a normative interface that includes an x402 scheme and a vault ABI; it is a design paper instantiated on the XDC Network, with evaluation deferred to follow-up work. The arXiv author metadata splits the first author's name into two single-word entries; it is recorded here as one name, as it appears on the abstract page.
whyItMatters: Argues that x402's atomic, final payments fit metered access but not refundable commerce, and shows how an escrow profile can still be exposed as an x402 scheme. x402: An application profile for refundable, delayed-fulfillment payments, a gap in x402 exact.

title: Here Come the Shopping Bots
summary: A research summary (2025-12-08) forecasting that agentic shoppers could account for $190 billion to $385 billion of US e-commerce spending by 2030, 10% to 20% of the market, and citing a survey in which about 23% of Americans bought something through AI in the past month.
whyItMatters: A mid-range market forecast with survey data on current AI-assisted buying; it marks how far analyst expectations sit from the small measured protocol volumes.

title: Agentic commerce and the battleground for new payments infrastructure
venue: Bank Underground (Bank of England staff blog)
summary: A Bank of England staff blog post (2026-05-21) on how agentic commerce could reshape payment design, stressing that deployers stay legally responsible for their agents and asking how existing frameworks apply to card, account-to-account and tokenized rails. Views are the author's, not the Bank's.
whyItMatters: Shows how a payment system operator and overseer frames the contest between card-network agent programs and newer rails such as stablecoin-based x402.

title: Verified by Visa and MasterCard SecureCode: Or, How Not to Design Authentication
venue: Financial Cryptography and Data Security 2010, LNCS
summary: Criticizes the original 3-D Secure schemes (Verified by Visa and MasterCard SecureCode) for training users to enter passwords into unverifiable inline frames, shifting liability onto cardholders, and weakening security in the name of convenience.
whyItMatters: 3-D Secure is the existing step-up and liability mechanism that card-based agent payments build on or bypass; this paper explains why authentication that users cannot verify fails. Visa Trusted Agent Protocol: Lessons from an earlier network-run authentication layer and its liability design.

title: Chip and PIN is Broken
venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy 2010
summary: Shows a man-in-the-middle attack on EMV chip cards in which a device between card and terminal makes the terminal believe the PIN was verified while the card believes signature verification was used, so a stolen card works with any PIN.
whyItMatters: A reminder that card security fails at the seams between parties that each see half the transaction; agent payment schemes add another party, the agent, between cardholder and merchant.

title: OpenID Connect for Agents (OIDC-A) 1.0: A Standard Extension for LLM-Based Agent Identity and Authorization
summary: Specifies OpenID Connect for Agents (OIDC-A) 1.0, an extension to OpenID Connect Core that adds standard claims, endpoints and flows for agent identity, attestation verification, delegation-chain validation and capability-based authorization while staying compatible with OAuth 2.0 infrastructure. A specification proposal is published on GitHub.
whyItMatters: A concrete OIDC-based alternative to the HTTP message signature approach of visa-tap and to the mandate chain in ap2. AP2: Agent identity extension for OpenID Connect.

title: The Case Against Micropayments
summary: Argues from pricing history that people prefer flat-rate and bundled pricing over metered charges, and that the mental cost of deciding on each tiny payment is the main obstacle to micropayments, not the technology.
whyItMatters: The classic objection to pay-per-use pricing; agent payments may sidestep it because software, not a person, makes each spending decision, which is the core bet behind x402 and MPP.

title: Trust and Task Completion in the World of Consumer AI Agents
summary: Proposes an evaluation that scores trust (nothing happens the user did not agree to, including spend limits and ignoring strangers' instructions) and task completion on the same runs in a simulated world of businesses with websites, inboxes and phone lines. The authors' assistant harness completes 71 percent of errands and keeps trust on 94 percent of trap runs versus 50 to 64 and 59 to 75 percent for base models; the study is a vendor evaluating its own product.
whyItMatters: Operationalizes the consumer-side guarantees that delegation designs such as AP2 intent and cart mandates and TAP promise, and shows how much of the result comes from the harness rather than the model.

title: AI Identity: Standards, Gaps, and Research Directions for AI Agents
summary: Defines AI identity as the continuous relationship between what an agent is declared to be and what it is observed to do, compares human and AI identity on substrate, persistence, verifiability and legal standing, evaluates current technical and regulatory documents against agent identity requirements, and identifies five structural gaps including recursive delegation accountability and agent identity integrity.
whyItMatters: A gap analysis that the identity claims in visa-tap, erc-8004 and ap2 can be checked against. Visa Trusted Agent Protocol: Survey of agent identity standards and gaps.

title: Micropayments for Decentralized Currencies
summary: Adapts probabilistic micropayments to decentralized currencies such as Bitcoin, designing schemes where a payer issues lottery-style tickets and only winning tickets are settled on chain, with protections against a payer who double-spends the escrow.
whyItMatters: Links the 1990s micropayment literature to blockchain settlement, the setting in which x402 operates and in which MPP offers on-chain payment methods.

title: Real AI Agents with Fake Memories: Fatal Context Manipulation Attacks on Web3 Agents
summary: Defines context manipulation (input channels, memory modules and external data feeds) as the attack surface of blockchain agents, shows on ElizaOS that injected prompts or falsified memories trigger unauthorized asset transfers, and introduces CrAIBench with over 150 Web3 tasks and over 500 attack cases. Memory injection proved more effective than prompt injection, and prompt-injection detectors offered little protection.
whyItMatters: The closest existing study of agents that hold crypto spending keys, the deployment model for x402 clients and ERC-8004 registered agents; a poisoned memory can drain a wallet that no protocol-level check would stop.

title: The Agentic Web Requires New Normative Infrastructure
summary: Argues that the agentic web needs normative infrastructure, laws, terms of service and norms that distinguish malicious bots from agents acting with a user's delegated authority, because platforms currently block or degrade agent access, often covertly; proposes normative principles and policies enabling appropriately delegated agents to act online.
whyItMatters: Policy context for visa-tap and openai-acp, which exist partly so that merchants can admit delegated agents while refusing abusive bots.

title: Can CaMeLs Talk? Securing Multi-Agent Systems Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks
summary: Shows that CaMeL's guarantees do not compose when agents call other agents as tools, because a downstream agent can reinterpret untrusted data as trusted input, and gives a concrete attack. Multi-CaMeL, an agent-to-agent protocol that passes untrusted data through a separate channel, brings attack success on MultiAgentDojo to 0.0 percent versus 0.2 percent for single-agent CaMeL and 12.9 percent undefended.
whyItMatters: Agent-to-agent commerce (A2A with x402, or buyer and merchant agents under ACP) is the hierarchical setting in which single-agent defenses fail; the protocol-level fix speaks to how payment messages between agents should be typed.

title: Web Agents Should Adopt the Plan-Then-Execute Paradigm
summary: Argues that ReAct is the wrong default for web agents because product pages mix seller, reviewer and advertiser content, and that agents should commit to a task program before seeing runtime content. All WebArena tasks fit plan-then-execute and 80 percent can run as pure programs; the barrier is that browser actions lack typed, semantic interfaces.
whyItMatters: Makes the case for typed, task-level commerce APIs, which is what UCP and OpenAI ACP provide in place of clicks: structured checkout interfaces are a security measure, not only a convenience.

title: The Bitcoin Lightning Network: Scalable Off-Chain Instant Payments
summary: The white paper (draft version 0.5.9.2, dated 2016-01-14) for a network of bidirectional payment channels in which transfers happen off chain and are routed across channels with hashed timelock contracts, so only channel opening and closing touch the blockchain.
whyItMatters: Payment channels are the main route to cheap, fast repeated payments; the deferred and session schemes discussed for x402 and MPP inherit the channel model this paper popularized.

title: AIP: Agent Identity Protocol for Verifiable Delegation Across MCP and A2A
summary: Introduces Invocation-Bound Capability Tokens, an append-only token chain that fuses identity, attenuated authorization and provenance binding, in a compact JWT mode and a chained Biscuit mode with Datalog policies for multi-hop delegation across MCP, A2A and HTTP. Python and Rust implementations add sub-millisecond overhead, and all 600 adversarial attempts were rejected.
whyItMatters: Delegation tokens for the A2A and MCP layers that ap2 and the a2a-x402 extension sit on, and a descendant of the Macaroons caveat model. AP2: Verifiable delegation across MCP and A2A.

title: Mandato: Protocol-Level Enforcement of Digitally Signed Mandates on AI Agent Actions with Cryptographically Chained Audit Trails
summary: Proposes a governance proxy that enforces signed, machine-readable mandates on MCP tool calls, blocking non-conforming calls and recording every decision in a hash-chained, timestamp-anchored audit trail. The mandate is modeled on the civil-law delegation of authority and mapped to EU AI Act, GDPR, NIS2 and eIDAS 2 obligations; the paper describes implementation status and an evaluation plan rather than results.
whyItMatters: A mandate concept parallel to AP2's intent and cart mandates, applied at the tool-call layer and tied to EU legal instruments, which is useful for the compliance view of delegation. AP2: Signed mandates enforced on tool calls, mapped to EU law.

title: Practical EMV Relay Protection
venue: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy 2022
summary: Analyzes relay attacks on contactless EMV, including a relay of Apple Pay transit transactions to locked iPhones, and proposes a relay protection protocol with a formal proof that would fit within existing EMV deployments.
whyItMatters: Relay is the card-present version of an agent acting far from the cardholder; the paper shows why binding a payment to its context, not just to valid credentials, matters.

title: LOKA Protocol: A Decentralized Framework for Trustworthy and Ethical AI Agent Ecosystems
summary: Presents the LOKA Protocol, a layered architecture with a Universal Agent Identity Layer for decentralized verifiable identity, intent-centric communication, and a Decentralized Ethical Consensus Protocol, anchored in DIDs, Verifiable Credentials and post-quantum cryptography.
whyItMatters: An identity and governance layer proposal that overlaps with the erc-8004 identity function; mostly conceptual.

title: Beyond DNS: Unlocking the Internet of AI Agents via the NANDA Index and Verified AgentFacts
summary: Describes the NANDA index architecture in which a lean index resolves to cryptographically verifiable AgentFacts supporting multi-endpoint routing, sub-second revocation and key rotation, schema-validated capability assertions and privacy-preserving discovery, with a CRDT-based update protocol and prototype resolvers.
whyItMatters: Another discovery and identity layer competing with erc-8004 registries; relevant to how agents find x402-priced services.

title: Reputation Systems
venue: Communications of the ACM, vol. 43, no. 12, pp. 45-48
summary: The classic statement of the problem: the Internet lets strangers transact at a scale where personal references and community standing no longer work, so reputation systems collect, aggregate and distribute feedback about past behavior. The authors set out what such systems must do and the difficulties of eliciting honest feedback and of cheap identity changes.
whyItMatters: ERC-8004's Reputation Registry is a reputation system in Resnick's sense, and the paper's warning about cheap identity changes is exactly the Sybil feedback dispute recorded against it.

venue: AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society (AIES 2025)
summary: Compares technical and legal ideas of agency, linking implied authority in agency law to value alignment in AI, and argues that computer science has under-theorized the agent's loyalty to its principal and its dealings with third parties.
whyItMatters: Agent payments put third parties (merchants, networks) in contact with an agent; the paper explains which legal duties may attach and why protocols record what the user actually authorized. AP2: Agency and liability when AI agents act.

title: Electronic lottery tickets as micropayments
summary: Proposes paying for many small items with electronic lottery tickets: each ticket wins a larger payment with small probability, so the expected value equals the price while the number of real transactions drops sharply.
whyItMatters: Probabilistic payment is one of the standing answers to per-request fees that are smaller than settlement cost, a problem x402 and MPP face whenever an agent buys thousands of cheap API calls.

summary: Introduces two micropayment schemes: PayWord, where a user commits to a hash chain and pays by revealing successive hash values, and MicroMint, where coins are hash collisions that are cheap to verify but costly to mint at scale. whyItMatters: The hash-chain idea behind PayWord is the template for streaming and session payments; MPP sessions and payment channels used with x402 apply the same principle of one setup and many cheap increments.
