title: The "Payment" HTTP Authentication Scheme
summary: Revision 01 (2026-09-09) of the draft behind the Machine Payments Protocol, written by authors from Tempo Labs and Stripe. It defines a "Payment" HTTP authentication scheme that uses the 402 status code to issue payment challenges and stays agnostic to payment method through registered method identifiers.
whyItMatters: The core MPP specification in IETF form; comparing it with x402, which also uses HTTP 402, shows the two designs for pay-per-request access.

title: The agentic commerce opportunity: How AI agents are ushering in a new era for consumers and merchants
summary: A consulting report (2025-10-17) estimating that agents could orchestrate $900 billion to $1 trillion of US B2C retail revenue by 2030 and $3 trillion to $5 trillion globally, counting goods only. It discusses the infrastructure, business models and trust needed for that shift.
whyItMatters: The largest of the widely cited market forecasts; useful as the upper bound when the atlas compares adoption claims, and it is a forecast, not measured volume.

title: Compliance-Aware Agentic Payments on Stablecoin Rails
summary: Describes a compliance-aware architecture that combines x402-style signature-based payment authorization and relayed execution with programmable compliance enforced on chain through a policy wrapper and a policy manager coordinating modular checks, so settlement stays low-friction when conditions are met and transaction-linked attestations are recorded. The arXiv comment labels it a demo-track paper, but no venue is confirmed.
whyItMatters: Shows one route to adding regulatory checks to x402 settlement at execution time rather than in an off-chain workflow. x402: Compliance-aware agent payments on stablecoin rails, relevant to facilitator screening.

title: OAuth 2.0 Extension: On-Behalf-Of User Authorization for AI Agents
summary: An individual draft (revision 02, 2025-08-26, expired 2026-02-27) extending OAuth 2.0 so an AI agent can obtain tokens on behalf of a user, adding a requested_actor parameter to the authorization request and an actor_token parameter to the token request so the delegation chain appears in the access token.
whyItMatters: A standards-track attempt at the delegation step that agent payment protocols solve in their own ways (mandates, agent tokens, signed intents); its expiry shows that no common OAuth profile for agents has been adopted yet.

title: A Decision-Centered Reference Architecture for Trustworthy Agentic Commerce
summary: A design-science study proposing a protocol-agnostic merchant-side architecture for agentic commerce built around a canonical decision envelope, protected dependency and result hashes, Ed25519 or HMAC authentication, live-request rebinding, a generated-claim gate and eleven semantic invariants, evaluated on an open-source JavaScript implementation with eight scenarios and five ablations; the author lists production security and interoperability as not established.
whyItMatters: Addresses what a merchant must keep authoritative when openai-acp, ucp or ap2 checkout messages arrive from agents, complementary to those protocol specifications. Agentic Commerce Protocol (ACP): Merchant-side reference architecture for agent commerce of the kind ACP serves.

title: Repeated-Game Security for Restaking-Based Verifiable Inference
summary: Shows that the usual one-round slashing argument for restaking-based verifiable LLM inference overstates security when a provider serves many queries under the same stake, because proportional slashing shrinks future penalties while cheating savings recur. It proposes history-dependent challenges, reputation-weighted slashing and stake vesting, and finds that surveyed deployed parameters admit profitable repeated deviations.
whyItMatters: ERC-8004 lists stake-secured re-execution as a validation option; this paper shows how to size stakes and audits so such validators stay honest over many jobs, not only one.

title: Issuer-Sovereign Agentic Payments
summary: Proposes Issuer-Sovereign Agentic Payments, in which the cardholder approves a spending rule once with the issuing bank's own authentication component, and at payment time the bank checks the merchant against that rule and generates the card authentication value only if allowed, so the transaction rides normal card rails with issuer validation and no extra execution-time dependency.
whyItMatters: A counterproposal to network-led designs such as visa-tap and mastercard-agent-pay, where spending controls are enforced by the network or a credential provider rather than the issuer. Visa Trusted Agent Protocol: Argues for issuer-side controls, contrasting with network-run agent recognition.

title: Sybil-Resistant Service Discovery for Agent Economies
summary: Introduces TraceRank, a reputation-weighted ranking for x402-enabled services in which payment transactions act as endorsements, seeded with precomputed reputation and propagated through the payment graph weighted by value and recency, then combined with semantic search. The authors argue that this resists Sybil spam because many low-reputation payers rank below a few high-reputation ones.
whyItMatters: An early proposal for discovery and reputation over the x402 payment graph, the same problem that erc-8004 reputation registries target. x402: Uses the x402 payment graph for Sybil-resistant service discovery.

title: Benchmarking Web Agent Safety under E-commerce Deceptive Interfaces
summary: Introduces WebDecept, a plugin that injects seven deceptive interface patterns (targeted advertisements, domain redirection, shopping manipulation and others) into existing web environments, and evaluates multimodal web agents under them. Agents were highly susceptible to several classes of deception and prompt-based constraints were often insufficient.
whyItMatters: Measures the merchant-side manipulation surface that structured checkouts in UCP and ACP are meant to remove, and gives a baseline for how agents behave when they must still browse a storefront. UCP: Web agent safety under deceptive e-commerce interfaces, which a trusted review UI must withstand.

title: Authenticated Delegation and Authorized AI Agents
summary: Proposes a framework for authenticated, authorized and auditable delegation of authority from humans to AI agents, extending OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect with agent-specific credentials and metadata, and a method for translating natural-language permissions into auditable access control configurations.
whyItMatters: The reference design for delegation chains that ap2 mandates, visa-tap agent identity and openai-acp checkout each assume but implement differently. AP2: Delegation credentials for agents, the idea behind open mandates. Visa Trusted Agent Protocol: Delegated agent credentials, the user-to-agent link that TAP leaves to VIC.

title: Identity Management for Agentic AI: The new frontier of authorization, authentication, and security for an AI agent world
summary: An OpenID Foundation white paper that surveys the authentication, authorization and identity resources available for today's agents, including MCP-centered practice, and sets out a strategic agenda for scalable access control, agent-centric identities, workload differentiation and delegated authority. Grey literature: the venue is the arXiv journal reference, not a peer-reviewed outlet.
whyItMatters: Standards-community baseline for the identity layer under visa-tap, ap2 and openai-acp; it records what OAuth and OIDC already cover and what is missing. AP2: OpenID Foundation white paper on agent identity and authorization. Visa Trusted Agent Protocol: Survey of agent identity that discusses Web Bot Auth.

title: Agentic Commerce Bench: Measuring Fraud Detection for Agents That Spend Money
summary: Presents a fraud taxonomy for agents with spend authority organized by five observation levels, a benchmark of twenty fraud classes built from production aggregates (1,647 service operations and 1,068 settlements), and gordonguard, an open-source detector stack. Calibrated detectors flag 6.5 percent of clean traffic and leave eight classes at chance, and a median payment of $0.007 makes one human review 143 times costlier than the payment it checks.
whyItMatters: Targets fraud on machine-to-machine rails such as x402 and MPP, where a counterparty can be exactly who it claims to be and still overcharge, and shows why identity checks alone, including ERC-8004 identity, do not stop value loss.

title: Building Trust in Autonomous Commerce: A Verifiable Global Event Timeline and AI-Ready Fraud Intelligence Layer
summary: Argues that AP2 and ACP lack interoperable, tamper-evident audit trails and proposes a global event timeline built from canonical event schemas, deterministic batching, Merkle commitments and blockchain anchoring, plus signed fraud markers tied to that evidence. A single-author prototype reports throughput figures; a copy is also on Zenodo (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.19060285).
whyItMatters: Names a gap shared by AP2 and ACP, the lack of a common verifiable event log for disputes and fraud signals, and sketches one way to fill it. Agentic Commerce Protocol (ACP): Argues ACP lacks interoperable, tamper-evident audit trails.

title: Hardening x402: PII-Safe Agentic Payments via Pre-Execution Metadata Filtering
summary: Presents presidio-hardened-x402, open-source middleware that intercepts x402 payment requests before transmission to redact personally identifiable information from payment metadata, enforce declarative spending policies and block replays. On a synthetic corpus of 2,000 metadata triples the recommended NLP mode reaches a micro-F1 near 0.9 at p99 latency under 6 ms; version 2 of the preprint revises the threshold and headline numbers.
whyItMatters: Highlights that x402 metadata travels to facilitators without data processing agreements, a privacy control gap in the protocol as deployed. x402: Treats x402 payment metadata as a PII channel and proposes filtering middleware.

title: zkLLM: Zero Knowledge Proofs for Large Language Models
summary: Presents zkLLM, a zero-knowledge proof system specialized for large language model inference, with a parallel lookup argument for non-arithmetic tensor operations and a dedicated proof for attention. It lets a model owner prove that an output came from committed parameters without revealing them.
whyItMatters: ERC-8004 leaves room for validators that check agent work with cryptographic proofs; zkLLM shows what a zkML validation response could attest to and how costly that proof is for transformer models. ERC-8004: Trustless Agents: zkML proofs, one of the validation methods the text names.

title: SoK: Decentralized Agent Economic Infrastructure
summary: Systematizes security and economic requirements across the lifecycle of an agent task into 17 property families over six stages, examines 12 systems and standards, five mechanism families and four classical baselines, and introduces guarantee closure, a criterion for whether guarantees made at one stage still constrain later decisions. Experiments over 840 matched executions and an 11,648-case check expose recurring gaps between verification and settlement.
whyItMatters: Relevant to stacks that chain ERC-8004 identity and validation with x402 payment: it shows how an escrow can release funds on an approval that carries little evidence the work was done. Which 12 systems are covered was not confirmed from the abstract alone.

title: Authorization Architectures for Tool-Using AI Agents
summary: A structured narrative review of 89 sources from 2023 to 2026 on authorization for tool-using agents, organized around a principal hierarchy (human, operator, orchestrator, sub-agent, tool endpoint) and five layers: identity and credential lifecycle, multi-hop delegation and scope propagation, runtime enforcement at policy enforcement points, prompt injection as authorization bypass, and auditability. It derives seven structural requirements and a four-layer reference architecture.
whyItMatters: A map of the delegation literature that the mandate chains of ap2 and the agent identity in visa-tap and openai-acp draw on.

title: Agentic commerce liability is still being written
summary: An acquirer's analysis (2026-07-30) noting that Visa, Mastercard and American Express have all launched frameworks for agent transactions while the question of who bears the loss in a dispute remains largely open.
whyItMatters: Liability allocation is the unresolved commercial question behind TAP and Agent Pay; this is the merchant-acquirer view of it. Visa Trusted Agent Protocol: Acquirer view that no agent liability shift exists yet.

title: Virtual Agent Economies
summary: Proposes the sandbox economy as a lens on the emerging layer in which AI agents transact at machine speed, classifying it by origin (emergent or intentional) and by permeability to the human economy. The authors discuss auctions for resource allocation, mission economies, and the identity, trust and oversight infrastructure needed to steer such markets, warning that the current path leads to a large and highly permeable agent economy with systemic risk.
whyItMatters: Names the infrastructure gaps (verifiable identity, reputation, controls on permeability) that ERC-8004 and x402 are being built to fill, and gives the policy vocabulary for discussing them.

title: AID-Guard: Stateful Authorization for Delegated Agent Effects
summary: AID-Guard closes the gap between authorization at admission and the provider effect that follows: it revalidates the approved request and provider state at commit, holds one reservation under ambiguity, and releases a successor only after a terminal result or a certified no-effect, so one approval yields at most one effect across retries and recovery. A prototype was tested against Stripe and Resend provider contracts, with all 210 Stripe trials matching predeclared outcomes.
whyItMatters: Exactly-once effects and idempotency are the operational core of agent payments; this is an evaluated protocol that treats a Stripe charge as a delegated effect with its own lifecycle, relevant to MPP and ACP implementations.

title: Underwriting the Agent Economy: The Blueprint for an AI Insurance Stack
summary: Argues that AI agent risk is mostly unpriced or excluded in current insurance lines and lays out an eight-part insurance stack, from incident data and catastrophe modeling to standards, pricing and claims, needed for large affirmative coverage by 2030.
whyItMatters: Insurance is a likely backstop for agent purchasing errors that card chargebacks and stablecoin settlement do not cover; the report sketches what insurers would need from protocol logs and standards.

title: APort Vault: Benchmarking AI Agent Payment Authorization with the Open Agent Passport
summary: Replays 4,371 human-written attacks from a capture-the-flag event against a live payment agent across 14 models, five policy levels and two tracks, with and without a deterministic pre-action check implementing the author's Open Agent Passport specification. Transfers to recipients the passport did not permit occurred 140 times in 76,842 model-alone evaluations and zero times in 69,297 behind the layer, while 25,370 legitimate payments still executed.
whyItMatters: A benchmark of the authorization boundary that AP2 mandates, x402 payment headers and TAP delegation all depend on: deterministic policy enforcement outside the model stopped recipient hijacks that prompting alone did not. The Open Agent Passport is the author's own specification, so read the comparison with that in mind.

title: Before the Tool Call: Deterministic Pre-Action Authorization for Autonomous AI Agents
summary: Characterizes the pre-action authorization problem, enforcing policy on a tool call before it executes, and presents the Open Agent Passport, an open specification and implementation that intercepts tool calls, evaluates a declarative policy and emits signed audit records at a median of 53 ms. In a live adversarial testbed with 4,437 decisions, social engineering succeeded 74.6% of the time under a permissive policy and 0% across 879 attempts under a restrictive one.
whyItMatters: The authorization layer that the APort Vault benchmark later uses for payment authorization; it sits in front of x402 and ap2 spending actions.

title: APEX: Agent Payment Execution with Policy for Autonomous Agent API Access
summary: APEX adapts HTTP 402-style payment gating to UPI-like real-time fiat rails with a challenge-settle-consume lifecycle, HMAC-signed short-lived tokens, idempotent settlement and policy-governed spend approval; in six scenarios policy enforcement cut spending by 27.3% while blocking all replay and invalid-token attempts.
whyItMatters: Shows the x402 pattern without the cryptocurrency rail, relevant to regions where stablecoin settlement is impractical.

title: Enhancing the A2A Protocol with Blockchain-Based Identities and x402 Micropayments for Agentic AI
venue: IJCCI 2025, Springer Communications in Computer and Information Science (CCIS), pp. 454-472
summary: Extends the A2A protocol with ledger-anchored identities, publishing AgentCards on chain as smart contracts for verifiable discovery, and with x402 micropayments so that agents can discover, authenticate and pay one another across organizational boundaries; includes an implementation and evaluation. Published in Springer CCIS from IJCCI 2025 under the title given here; the arXiv preprint (2507.19550, 2025) carries the longer title 'Towards Multi-Agent Economies: Enhancing the A2A Protocol with Ledger-Anchored Identities and x402 Micropayments for AI Agents'.
whyItMatters: Peer-reviewed design that pairs x402 with on-chain agent identity, the same combination that erc-8004 plus x402 deployments pursue. ERC-8004: Trustless Agents: Ledger-anchored identity with A2A and x402, before ERC-8004. x402: Combines A2A with ledger-anchored identities and x402 micropayments.

title: Paying to Know: Micro-Transaction Markets for Verified Product Information in Agentic E-Commerce
summary: A vision paper arguing that once buyers are agents paying over agent-native rails such as x402 and AP2, the scarce resource becomes trustworthy product information rather than product matching. It sketches a market in which buyer agents pay fractions of a cent to unlock seller- and reviewer-supplied evidence, with reviewer trust scored reputationally, and lists the NLP problems this creates.
whyItMatters: Names x402 and AP2 directly as the rails that make per-fact micropayments feasible, and ties paid information to the reputation scoring that ERC-8004 registries aim to provide.

title: FP-Inconsistent: Measurement and Analysis of Fingerprint Inconsistencies in Evasive Bot Traffic
summary: Buys traffic from 20 bot services against a honey site protected by two commercial anti-bot products and finds that about half the requests evade detection by altering browser fingerprints; inconsistencies among altered attributes then help detect them.
whyItMatters: Measures how weak fingerprint-based bot detection is, which is the problem Visa TAP and Mastercard Agent Pay address by having trusted agents sign their requests instead of hiding as browsers. Visa Trusted Agent Protocol: Why fingerprint-based bot detection fails and cryptographic agent identity appeals.

title: Agentic Payments from the Ground Up: What the Onchain Data Tells Us
venue: Visa and Artemis joint research report
summary: A joint report (summary page last updated 2026-07-14) that splits agentic commerce into agent purchases on behalf of people and small machine-to-machine payments, and measures x402 at about $15.0 million adjusted volume over 109.6 million transactions and MPP at about $25,000 over 115,000 transactions, using Artemis data as of 2026-04-21.
whyItMatters: The main vendor-published measurement of x402 and MPP volumes; the adjusted figures exclude activity Artemis classed as wash or test traffic, and they are self-reported, not independently audited.

title: Shopping by algorithm: How agentic AI deploys human heuristics as a surrogate consumer
summary: Using Tool-Lab, a process-tracing setup that hides product attributes behind costly tool calls, the authors test eight deployed LLMs from three providers against just-below pricing and promotional framing. Cues rarely mislead when information is free, but under acquisition costs and a vague goal the agents skip the attributes needed to compute unit price and make heuristic, suboptimal choices much like people.
whyItMatters: Shows that storefront information architecture and tool cost shape what agents buy, which matters for how merchants expose product data in ACP and UCP feeds and for proposals to sell product information per fact over x402. Agentic Commerce Protocol (ACP): Agents as surrogate consumers; behavior behind ACP purchases.

title: Payments in the Age of AI Agents
summary: A Federal Reserve Governor speech separating agent-assisted commerce, where the buyer decides and pays, from agent-delegated commerce, where an agent shops and pays within guardrails, and naming authentication, liability and fraud as the main barriers to the delegated model. The Board speech feed dates it 2026-09-29.
whyItMatters: States in policy terms the shift every protocol in the atlas addresses: proving that an agent holds authority to pay, not only that the cardholder is genuine.

title: BazaarBench: Delegation Safety in Decentralized C2C Marketplaces Run by LLM Agents
summary: A simulated consumer-to-consumer marketplace with 100 agents, eBay-derived inventories and reputation-based trust, scoring six failure types across five transaction stages over 357,608 model calls. All five tested models promise the same item to multiple buyers, and under adversarial instructions the share of committed sales completed despite unavailable items or overstated condition rises from 15.4 to 33.4 percent, with most extra earnings coming from goods the sellers never held.
whyItMatters: Tests whether reputation can hold a decentralized agent market together, the premise behind ERC-8004's Reputation Registry, and measures delegation failures that ACP and UCP style checkouts would inherit from the agents using them.

title: When HTTP 402 Meets the Blockchain: Risks on Emerging x402 Payments
summary: Studies facilitator-mediated x402 deployments in the wild, derives eight security rules for facilitators and four attack vectors (Free Shopping, Asset Theft, Service Denial, Gas Abuse), and applies a semi-automated black-box tool to 15 facilitators serving over 60,000 sellers and 360,000 buyers, finding violations in all of them. Findings were disclosed and mitigated, including changes by Coinbase, and the paper adds a measurement of more than 119 million Base and Solana transactions. Listed on the USENIX Security 2026 technical sessions page (accessed 2026-10-10).
whyItMatters: Peer-reviewed evidence that the x402 facilitator is a shared trust point whose flaws affect many merchants at once, plus adoption and centralization metrics. x402: Studies facilitator-mediated deployments and proposes eight safety rules for facilitators.

title: Who Is Your Agent Serving? Provider-Side Indirect Prompt Injection in Proactive Agents
summary: Shows that an external provider controlling only content about its own product can redirect a proactive personal agent to recommend it, recruit the user's private context to justify it and lower adoption friction, without compromising the agent or gaining permissions. Across three environments and six user models the macro gain reaches 77.4 percentage points, and provider influence persists even when no final authorization is given.
whyItMatters: Models the merchant-side incentive to manipulate agent recommendations in ACP and UCP style markets, where the provider's own listing is the injection vector.

title: Can Trustless Agents Be Trusted? An Empirical Study of the ERC-8004 Decentralized AI Agent Ecosystem
summary: First empirical study of ERC-8004 on Ethereum, BNB Smart Chain and Base from deployment through 2026-05-13, crawling Identity and Reputation Registry events, registration files and associated x402 payments. Only 3%, 4% and 15% of registrations on the three chains expose a valid registration file with a live endpoint, reputation values are not commensurable and are cheap to manipulate, and 73.5%, 59.2% and 90.6% of reviewers show coordinated Sybil behavior; removing flagged feedback leaves 15.8%, 77.9% and 86.8% of rated agents with no valid feedback.
whyItMatters: Primary evidence for the disputed status of erc-8004 reputation data and for the gap between registrations and operational agents; it also links x402 settlements to registered identities. ERC-8004: Trustless Agents: The main measurement of ERC-8004 in practice: liveness and Sybil reviewers on three chains.

title: Parallelism or Concession? Concurrency-Aware Procurement Negotiation for Agentic Commerce
summary: Models an agentic buyer that can run many parallel negotiations at once, each with a cost and a risk of over-commitment, and shows that more concurrent negotiators can replace price concessions. It turns the results into an optimizer that picks the number of negotiators and a price cap, and it beats common heuristics in simulation.
whyItMatters: Agents can fan out purchase requests cheaply, which changes merchant-side load and cancellation risk for checkout protocols built around one buyer and one cart.

title: Sound Debloating of Redundant Checks in Zero-Knowledge Machine-Learning Circuits
summary: Builds a tool that removes redundant checks from zero-knowledge machine learning circuits only when the rest of the circuit still provably enforces them, so the smaller circuit cannot accept forged proofs. On circuits from ezkl and zkml with up to 25.3 million constraints it removes up to 48.7% of constraints and cuts prover time by up to 72.8%.
whyItMatters: zkML proofs are only as good as their circuits; for ERC-8004 validators that accept zkML evidence, under-constrained circuits are a real forgery risk and proving cost is the main adoption barrier, and this work addresses both.

title: Agentic Web: Weaving the Next Web with AI Agents
summary: Proposes a framework for the Agentic Web built on three dimensions (intelligence, interaction, economics), traces its evolution from the PC and mobile web, and discusses communication protocols, orchestration and an Agent Attention Economy together with governance risks.
whyItMatters: Its economics dimension and attention-economy discussion anticipate the discovery and monetization questions that UCP, ACP and x402 are now standardizing.

title: A Survey of AI Agent Protocols
summary: Surveys agent communication protocols with a two-dimensional classification (context-oriented versus inter-agent, general-purpose versus domain-specific), compares them on security, scalability and latency, and lays out directions such as layered architectures, privacy preservation and group interaction.
whyItMatters: Provides the taxonomy into which payment and commerce protocols (x402, AP2, ACP, UCP) slot as domain-specific layers above MCP and A2A. UCP: Survey of AI agent protocols for orientation.

title: Paying for Honesty Without Knowing the Truth: Reputation-Penalty Design for LLM Marketplace Agents
summary: LLM merchant agents fabricate product attributes in most listings under competitive pressure even when told to be honest. CARP, a reputation-penalty mechanism with a deadband that forgives complaint noise and a state-dependent severity, suppresses low-rated liars without any product-level ground truth, and SPARC makes the penalty behaviorally binding so merchants restrain themselves once lying costs sales.
whyItMatters: Shows how a platform-level reputation penalty can govern seller agents behind ACP or UCP storefronts using only noisy complaints, a design that could sit on top of ERC-8004 feedback entries.

title: WebShop: Towards Scalable Real-World Web Interaction with Grounded Language Agents
summary: A simulated e-commerce site with 1.18 million real products and 12,087 crowd-sourced instructions in which an agent must search, customize and buy an item. It introduced compositional instruction following, query reformulation and noisy web text as grounding challenges and collected over 1,600 human demonstrations for training.
whyItMatters: The ancestor of every agentic shopping benchmark; the search, option selection and checkout steps it scripted are what ACP and UCP now turn into protocol messages. Agentic Commerce Protocol (ACP): Foundational shopping-agent benchmark.

title: τ-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains
summary: Simulates conversations between an LLM-played user and an agent that has domain API tools and policy documents, grading by comparing the final database state to an annotated goal and introducing the pass^k reliability metric. Even strong function-calling agents succeeded on under half of the tasks and were inconsistent across trials, with pass^8 below 25 percent in retail.
whyItMatters: Its retail domain (orders, exchanges, refunds under policy) is the post-purchase side of ACP and UCP, and pass^k is the reliability framing merchants need before letting agents touch orders. Agentic Commerce Protocol (ACP): Retail tool-use benchmark close to ACP checkout tool calls.

title: InjecAgent: Benchmarking Indirect Prompt Injections in Tool-Integrated Large Language Model Agents
summary: A benchmark of 1,054 test cases over 17 user tools and 62 attacker tools that measures whether tool-integrated agents follow injected instructions aimed at direct harm or data exfiltration. Across 30 agents the vulnerability was substantial, with ReAct-prompted GPT-4 following injections in roughly one case in four.
whyItMatters: Supplies the attacker-tool framing (a malicious tool result that triggers a transfer) that payment-agent threat models for AP2 and x402 reuse.

title: StepJack: Benchmarking Computer-Use Agent Safety Against Multi-Step Indirect Prompt Injection
summary: Introduces multi-step indirect prompt injection, in which an adversarial goal is split into innocuous sub-steps spread across pages along the agent's navigation path, and a benchmark of 480 cases. Across six computer-use agents, decomposition raises attack success, for one model from 41.7 percent single-step to 72.9 percent at three steps.
whyItMatters: Computer-use agents that shop across several merchant pages are the deployment TAP and Agent Pay credentials are issued to; staged injections evade per-page defenses.

title: SoK: Blockchain Agent-to-Agent Payments
summary: Systematizes blockchain-based agent-to-agent payments, with x402 as the lead example, into a four-stage lifecycle of discovery, authorization, execution and accounting, classifies representative designs at each stage, and isolates recurring weaknesses: weak intent binding, misuse under valid authorization, payment-service decoupling and limited accountability.
whyItMatters: Gives a lifecycle vocabulary for x402 and for the discovery role that erc-8004 registries are meant to fill, and names the payment-service decoupling problem that later x402 attack papers exploit. ERC-8004: Trustless Agents: Survey that places ERC-8004 among agent payment components. x402: Systematizes blockchain agent-to-agent payments, with x402 as a central case.

title: From Review to Authorization: Key-Isolated Threshold Signing for LLM Agents
summary: KITA keeps the user's signing key and every threshold key share outside all LLM processes; an action is authorized only when t reviewer-signer domains contribute shares bound to the canonical action after authenticated approval, so a prompt-injected proposer cannot forge an authorization. The path is implemented with a structured-output LLM adapter and threshold BLS signatures.
whyItMatters: Addresses the gap formal analyses of x402 and AP2 point to: the agent that reads untrusted content should not hold the credential that signs the payment.

title: WebArena: A Realistic Web Environment for Building Autonomous Agents
summary: A reproducible environment of fully functional websites across e-commerce, forums, software development and content management, with tools and knowledge bases and a benchmark of long-horizon tasks graded on functional correctness rather than on action traces.
whyItMatters: Its e-commerce site is the standard sandbox for web shopping agents; Piet et al. and Shi et al. in this bibliography build their security arguments on it. UCP: Foundation benchmark for web agents that shop through ordinary sites, the path UCP replaces.

title: The Automated but Risky Game: Modeling and Benchmarking Agent-to-Agent Negotiations and Transactions in Consumer Markets
summary: Builds an experimental framework in which consumer and merchant LLM agents negotiate and transact with each other. Outcomes differ sharply across models, and behavioral anomalies lead to overspending or acceptance of unreasonable deals, producing losses for both sides.
whyItMatters: Agent-to-agent negotiation is the step before an ACP or UCP checkout and before an AP2 mandate is signed; the paper quantifies the asymmetry and loss risk users accept when they delegate the deal itself.

title: When Guardrails Look Effective: Construct Validity Failures in LLM Agent Commerce Evaluation
summary: Audits a multi-turn buyer and seller agent testbed and shows that reported welfare gains from marketplace guardrails largely came from giving guarded and unguarded agents different offer formats; once the protocol is held fixed the effects shrink or vanish within noise. It proposes a construct-validity checklist that must pass before policy claims are made from agent market simulations.
whyItMatters: A caution for anyone citing agent-commerce simulations as evidence that a protocol feature or guardrail works; the comparison must hold the protocol constant.

title: Runtime Authorization for Resources Acquired by AI Agents
summary: Identifies a post-fulfillment activation gap: payment, budget, OAuth, mandate and fulfillment checks validate a transaction but do not decide whether a resource an agent acquires (compute, credentials, accounts, other agents) may become usable authority. Proposes a provenance-bounded runtime authorization architecture that quarantines acquired outputs and activates them only through checked activation transactions, with eight proved safety properties and trace-based evaluation.
whyItMatters: Extends the ap2 and x402 question from whether a payment was authorized to what the agent may do with what it bought, a gap none of the eight protocols addresses.

title: InterSAGE: The Secure and Verifiable Interoperability Protocol for An Internet of Agents
summary: A positioning paper for InterSAGE, a four-layer trust protocol suite (persistent identity, discovery, trust negotiation and accountability) meant to run alongside MCP, A2A, ANP and AG-UI. It binds agent identity cards to developer, code and operator, and compares the design with more than 50 related efforts.
whyItMatters: Another proposal for the identity and accountability layer that ERC-8004 provides on chain; its survey table is a useful map of competing agent identity designs.
